you. On the use of this pronoun see what I said under ἐγώ [I] p. 99. The Aeschylean examples arranged according to the order of cases are these.

The oblique cases are either orthotone σοῦ σοί σέ [of you, to you, you], or enclitic σου σοι σε [of you, to you, you], with the accent thrown back onto the preceding word. The proper use of the orthotone forms is when they are constructed with prepositions according to the rule of the grammarians, although not entirely true, about which I spoke in the Lexicon Sophocleum under ἐγώ [I] p. 134 b.
The epic form of the genitive is σέθεν [of you], which the tragedians use in dialogue as well as in lyric passages when the meter demands it.
The dative is either orthotone σοί [to you] or enclitic σοι [to you], which differ in the same way as σοῦ and σου [of you], about which we spoke above. Both occur in the same sentence.
The accusative is either orthotone σέ [you] or enclitic σε [you], which differ as σοῦ σου [of you] and σοί σοι [to you], about which we spoke above.
There is one example of the dual number.
Of the accusative ὔμμε [you], which epic and lyric poets use, there is one example in a trimeter.

Words compounded with σύν [with] and this preposition itself, since in the manuscripts of the scenic poets they are written sometimes one way, sometimes the other, with the meter demanding either one spelling or the other, or allowing both, we present all these under the letter σ.
Always indeed you are pitiless and full of boldness.
But do not toil in vain over things that are of no help.
And have you indeed come as an overseer of my toils?

But you, child, do not spurn the marriage bed.
But you, Inachian seed, cast my words into your heart.
